tension: Job seekers grind through months or years of applications in a brutal, hiring-averse market yet still can't land a job.
Workers and candidates feel employers and clients deliberately pay or offer them less than their experience and real market value are worth.
Job seekers are frustrated that hiring filters reject competent candidates on shallow proxies (a missing degree, keyword/AI scans, resume gaps) instead of actual ability.
Someone being harassed or abused (online or at work) can't figure out how to safely shut the person down or protect themselves without making the situation worse.
Job seekers feel applying online is a hopeless numbers game where they're just one of thousands, so they scramble for any edge — applying first, staying visible — just to avoid being ignored.
The relentless pace, long hours, understaffing and always-on demands burn workers out and leave them no work-life balance, so they long for a way out of the grind.

phrases.phrase: good work punished with more work

tension: Service providers struggle to charge and hold fair prices because clients constantly lowball, haggle, guilt-trip, and demand discounts.
Tech workers are frustrated that relentless mass layoffs have destroyed the job security that even big-tech and once-stable roles used to guarantee.
Hiring teams can't trust code submissions as a skill signal because candidates hand in AI-generated or copied code they can't explain or actually understand.
Job seekers resent that gaps and breaks in their work history get stigmatized and interrogated by employers, forcing them to justify or disguise time away from work.

Workers are being laid off — juniors and engineers especially — with AI named as the reason, so people resent AI being used as cover or justification for cutting jobs whether or not it can actually do the work.
People who invested in a CS degree or tech career are frustrated that it no longer delivers the prestige, security, or wealth it once promised.
Job seekers get rejected for reasons that feel arbitrary or outside their control — too eager, too qualified, wrong 'vibe' or culture fit, their grades, or a keyword filter.

US tech workers are frustrated that companies are laying them off and replacing them with cheaper foreign labor — either shipping jobs offshore or exploiting H-1B visas — instead of hiring domestic workers.
Workers feel treated as disposable while executives cut staff to pad their own bonuses and dodge the layoffs they caused.

Outside applicants feel the game is rigged — jobs are quietly locked up by internal candidates, referrals, and personal connections (or decided early on gut feel) before merit or an open application ever counts.
Job seekers resent having to reverse-engineer keywords and file formats just so an automated ATS will pass their resume to a human at all.
Employees feel HR sides with the company — enforcing discipline, guarding liability, and even betraying or dismissing worker complaints — instead of protecting the people it claims to serve.
Job-seekers are ghosted or left waiting as recruiters and employers go silent or stall on them while applying, interviewing, and even after an offer.

Job seekers feel deceived when a posting sells a role that turns out to be false — a 'remote' job that isn't, a misrepresented location or pay, terms that change mid-process, or a position that never really existed.
Job candidates feel disrespected and demeaned by the way recruiters and interviewers communicate — harsh, judgmental, insulting, and unprofessional.
New and aspiring tech workers are frustrated that entry-level hiring has collapsed, leaving CS grads unemployed and early-career IT roles hard to land, advance in, or earn a living wage from.
Employers screen out or reject people based on age or other protected traits when hiring.
The interview process drags on with too many rounds and stages, keeping candidates and employers stuck in a slow, bloated pipeline for months.
Job candidates are frustrated that assessments test framing, personality, or reading-comprehension instead of the actual skill the role needs.
Job-seekers' resumes get auto-screened out or ignored without a human ever reading them, so qualified applicants never surface or land interviews.
People caught in a firing fear the process is an adversarial, legally-loaded setup where a paper trail or sham PIP is built to justify pushing them out.
Employers are being cheated out of the hours and money they pay for, by employees who lie about time worked and fake the expenses they claim.
People with no prior experience are locked out of entry-level jobs because those jobs demand years of experience they can't get without a job.
Job seekers can't agree whether rewriting their resume for each specific role is worth the effort or a waste of time.
Job seekers wrestle with how much to inflate and aggressively self-promote on a resume to look impressive without crossing into dishonesty.
Business owners fear that a slowing, uncertain economy makes this the wrong time to build, invest, or commit resources.

Romantic or sexual relationships between coworkers — especially across a manager-subordinate power gap — force agonizing decisions about whether to disclose, and blow up into scandal when they surface.
Workers are let go with no warning or human decency — finding out through a text, an email, a stopped paycheck, or by accident instead of a real conversation.

Employees' personal time and legitimate absences are disregarded or punished by the employer — from a minute's lateness to bereavement, holidays, a single absence, notice periods, and maternity leave.
Vague, feelings-based answers don't land, so people struggle to make their case with hard data, numbers, and clear structure.
Candidates get flagged and rejected on assumptions about their character, personal life, or likelihood of leaving rather than on their ability to do the job.
People are cynical about self-serving PR and promotion stunts that ring hollow, spam, and can't even be measured.
Employers can't trust that applicants are who they claim, because candidates fake their identities, credentials, and resumes to get hired.
Honest negative feedback about an employer or worker backfires — it gets filtered, disputed, or answered with retaliation, so the truth stays buried and speaking up is punished.
Employers dread the candidate or new hire whose toxic character — arrogant, dishonest, abusive, or culturally aggressive — outweighs their qualifications.
Employers deny employees the pay, leave, accommodations, and medical privacy the law entitles them to.
Workers doubt whether six figures is actually reachable — especially without a degree — when help-desk pay rarely gets there and hitting 100k seems to require job-hopping.
Job seekers feel dehumanized because commission and KPI-driven recruiters treat them as targets and props rather than people, so empathy and accountability disappear.
Workers are pressured to put in extra hours and labour that their pay never covers, so they're effectively working part of the time for free.
Rejections arrive cold and impersonal — mass form emails, no real feedback, or a reply years too late — leaving candidates without closure or a reason.
Job seekers are frustrated that pay is kept hidden and taboo, wanting ranges disclosed upfront instead of having to pry them out.
Developers are fed up that AI-assisted 'vibe coding' ships low-quality slop that breaks in production, deserving the mockery it gets.
Devs argue the coding is the easy part while the real, unautomatable difficulty (understanding requirements, solving the problem, writing clearly) is what goes unrewarded.
Readers are frustrated that online communities are flooded with low-quality AI-generated posts that pose as genuine human writing, so they can't trust that any post is real.
Job seekers are actively defrauded by criminal scams disguised as recruitment — fake interviews, malware, and paid upsell traps.
Workers are frustrated that startups demand toxic, grinding conditions while offering unstable jobs and equity that rarely pays off.
People struggle to turn cold outreach into genuine professional relationships, so generic messages fail and only personalized, rapport-building contact lands.
Professionals are bombarded by unprofessional, impersonal recruiter outreach and want to shut it off.
Remote video interviews turn awkward and unprofessional — interruptions, distractions, bad backgrounds, and on-the-spot mishaps.
Applicants find there are no real openings to apply to — roles are already filled, there's no headcount, and the 'talent shortage' is a myth.
Workers feel controlled and mistreated by their employer during the exit itself, from forced notice periods to loyalty going unrewarded and exit-interview rituals.
Job-seekers are frustrated that formal credentials (degree, GPA, résumé, qualifications) count for far less than proof you can actually do the work.
Workers are frustrated that being liked, visible, and well-presented gets rewarded more than doing the real work well.
A company's best and most experienced people keep leaving, and the churn hollows out its mentorship and culture while the replacements can't match them.
Screening rewards the wrong signal (polished code output, ATS keywords, boolean matches) so genuinely capable people get filtered out while the screen misses real ability.
AI makes coding look faster than it really is but produces buggy, insecure code that engineers must review and fix under rising expectations.
People resent that management ceremony — standups, stakeholder updates, productivity metrics — becomes overhead and status-theater instead of reflecting real work done.
Service providers keep getting stiffed or walked over by clients, so they feel forced to defensively lock everything down before doing the work.
People resent that polishing their communication into professional corporate-speak (often via AI) makes them sound fake and inhuman instead of authentically themselves.
Employees are frustrated that staying and performing well earns no raise, so the only way to get paid more is to threaten to quit or actually leave.
Job seekers waste effort on listings that aren't genuine hires because recruiters and companies post fake, ghost, or misrepresented jobs.
Workers can only win real pay raises by switching jobs, yet employers stigmatize that and demand a steady, loyal work history.
Employees resent bosses who police attendance and presence and take boundaries personally instead of trusting them to just do the work.
Job seekers pour money and time into certifications to get hired and doubt whether the credentials actually pay off.
The offer stage turns adversarial — a lowball, a counter, arrogance, or a stall blows up the deal and someone walks.
Managers find that real leadership rests on hard-won trust, and carrying that trust is its own weight.
Speaking uncomfortable truths — blunt feedback, unspoken concerns, owning your own mistakes — is valued yet risky and hard to sit with.
People wrestle with trusting their own gut and taking career risks instead of waiting for permission or outside validation.
Candidates resent that interviews force them to put on a fake performance — a costume, a script, an act — instead of being an honest exchange.
Job-seekers earned the certs and degrees they were told to get, but still can't land a job or a decent salary.
Departing workers worry they will be cheated out of the pay and benefits they are owed when they leave a job.
A business is trapped by dependence on one dominant customer or single market that can dictate bad payment terms because losing them would be devastating.
Both recruiters and candidates have automated outreach and applications with AI, so hiring has decayed into bots messaging and answering bots and flooding everyone's inboxes.
Managers and HR are frustrated by having to document and handle complaints exactly right — confidential, in writing, independently investigated — to avoid retaliation and liability.
People can't trust reviews and compliance reports because they're routinely bought, faked, or suppressed.
Engineers are frustrated that getting recognized and promoted requires actively self-marketing (brag docs, visibility tactics, emailing execs) rather than the work speaking for itself.
Job candidates get asked intrusive, legally off-limits personal questions during interviews.
Recruiters waste time screening a flood of mismatched applicants (unqualified juniors and overqualified candidates) who don't fit the role.
Even people who have work face income that is unstable and never enough, forcing second jobs or leaving them anxious and stuck in low pay.
Interviews lean on canned questions and surface rituals instead of a real, performance-based conversation that reveals the actual candidate.
Disillusioned workers are pulling back and doing the bare minimum, quietly disengaging and showing up only for the paycheck.
Workers are frustrated by managers who don't actually manage — glorified babysitters padding their stats and sitting above their competence while adding no value.
Deserving employees are denied the promotion or recognition they were owed.
The candidate is the one who says no — declining or withdrawing from an employer they no longer want.
Candidates resent being kept as a fallback — a second choice or backup held in reserve while the employer really wants someone else, often an internal hire.
Employers lose candidates who take themselves out of the running — dropping out, pricing themselves out, or self-sabotaging — instead of being actively chosen or rejected.
Job seekers are unsure which personal details actually help versus hurt and should be left off a resume.
The lone HR practitioner is stretched across an entire company's HR function alone and burning out under it.
Support staff are frustrated that users won't use the self-service tools and instead flood them with trivial requests they could handle themselves.
Skilled engineers are worn down by constant interrupt-driven low-level ticket work and wish for help to offload the grind.
The team depends on one person who holds all the knowledge with no documentation or trained backup, turning them into a bottleneck.
AI is overhyped and doesn't deliver the promised productivity gains, so people feel the hype is dying and the money poured in was misallocated.
AI generates low-quality 'slop' that experienced people are forced to clean up, which slows them down and degrades the software instead of improving it.
A product's quality steadily declines until users abandon it.
The person doing the firing loses control of it — freezing up, getting lawyered up, having the fallout reach the employee's family, or realizing too late who they let go.
The AI job market has become a frenzy of inflated pay, talent poaching, and AI-first listings that many suspect is a bubble.
Developers feel pressured to build side projects and portfolios on their own time just to prove they're worth hiring.
Skilled professionals struggle to turn their existing experience into an independent income stream of clients, products, or an audience.
Startup founders are frustrated that the H-1B visa fee hike makes hiring foreign talent unaffordable and threatens small companies' survival.
Solo operators and small businesses are anxious about personal legal exposure and scramble to shield themselves before a lawsuit hits.
People are terrified of wiping themselves out financially by going all-in on a venture instead of keeping a buffer and proving real income first.
Citizens have no way to see where public/road contract money goes, so corrupt contractors escape accountability.
Older workers are frustrated that their resume betrays their age and gets them screened out before anyone looks at their skill.
Workers are frustrated that their role is being eliminated (handed to AI or a pod) even though their performance is still fine.
Remaining employees are frustrated that departed roles aren't backfilled, so the extra work just gets dumped onto them.
People are frustrated that no career field is a safe bet anymore because the jobs aren't coming back and every alternative saturates.
Employers can't trust that the person logging in is who they claim to be, because credentials and identities are being borrowed, stolen, or leaked.
Workplaces are unprepared to keep people safe or respond when an emergency happens.
The channels for applying have become a gatekept hassle — you can't apply in person, you're pushed to apply directly on company sites, and some places even make you pay to apply.
Job seekers can't find out what a role actually pays because salary is hidden until a call and endlessly qualified as 'depends on the company/sector.'
Candidates are frustrated that interviews treat them as the only party being judged, when they should be able to size up the employer's culture in return.
Essential and low-wage workers aren't paid a living wage, so they labour just to survive while their work goes unseen and undervalued.
Workers live in constant fear of losing their jobs amid endless budget cuts and layoffs.
Employees wrestle with the guilt and relief of leaving a manager — escaping toxic ones while feeling bad about leaving good ones.
Employees are pressured to lie on the job and pay the price when the lie surfaces.
Candidates want to be judged on honest, authentic answers rather than a rehearsed performance or surface appearances.
Developers resent having to sink endless, ongoing hours into leetcode drilling just to stay interview-ready.
Recruiters can't get candidates and developers to respond to their cold outreach and InMails.
Candidates struggle with nerves and rustiness that sabotage how they come across in interviews.
People distrust the pay figures quoted during negotiation because both sides fake salary ranges and competing offers to gain leverage.
Employers resent the fees recruiters and search firms charge and push to negotiate that cost down.
People pushed out involuntarily struggle to rebuild and find new work in the aftermath of being fired or laid off.
Sales and recruitment reps are angry that employers retroactively cut or claw back the commission they already earned.
People are subjected to unwanted advances and inappropriate behavior from colleagues or their own managers.
HR's professional worth is dismissed as a valueless cost center that generates no revenue and contributes nothing anyone respects.
Skilled builders are frustrated at being pushed into supervisory or management roles when they just want to keep building.
Engineers want the authority to own and merge their own work instead of being gatekept by someone else's approval.
The whole AI push feels ethically wrong to people, like tech has abandoned any ethics and is spiraling toward a bad end.
The company won't develop its people, so staff stay untrained, unable to work independently, and their potential goes wasted.
A startup is fragile and collapses, whether from founder conflict or the odds that most simply fail.
Employees' documented medical needs and accommodation requests are ignored or refused when they try to keep working.
People are frustrated that commercial pitches disguised as genuine community posts (native ads, influencers hawking courses, planted reviews) are manipulating them.
Recruiters are frustrated that candidates use AI to fake their identity or presence in interviews, so they can't trust who they're actually hiring.
People feel on the back foot in tough conversations and negotiations, unsure how to deliver hard messages without losing leverage or goodwill.
Developers distrust AI producing real code and communication autonomously, wanting it confined to boilerplate rather than pushing pull requests and writing replies.
Salespeople are frustrated that quotas and commission targets are set so high that nobody can actually hit them.
Workers are frustrated that return-to-office is about optics and visibility, not any real need to be in the building.
Job seekers are frustrated that postings are shams because the pick (often a relative) is already made and the req was never truly open.
Employees are frustrated that advertised benefits are illusory, coming with hidden caps and no legal guarantee behind them.
Companies and individuals inflate their own titles and certifications to appear more legitimate and qualified than they really are.
Hiring managers are too busy and unavailable to interview, becoming the bottleneck that stalls hiring.
Recruiters lose scheduled candidates to interview no-shows and lean on reminder texts to stop the drop-off.
Return-to-office mandates strip away the flexibility workers built their lives around, pushing them to disengage.
Paid-time-off policies breed friction — unlimited PTO no one feels free to use, and resentment toward coworkers who take theirs.
Physically demanding jobs grind down the worker's body over the years.
Job seekers are angry at discriminatory hiring where employers only hire single guys or refuse to hire Indians.
People resent entitled, out-of-touch elites whose elite education breeds hypocrisy rather than humility.
Workers struggle to recognize toxic workplaces, and find finally leaving them a relief.
People do everything right and still get punished for it.
Recruiters get ghosted by the candidates and clients they were already actively engaged with.
Candidates are frustrated that companies extract unpaid labor through interview assignments and write-ups.
Interviewers are frustrated that candidates game or cheat their way through interviews, letting unqualified people pass.
Older applicants strip their graduation year off their resume to dodge age discrimination.
Employers refuse to invest anything in new workers — no training and unpaid internships.
Job seekers struggle to make their LinkedIn profile actually pull its weight in the job hunt.
People can't get honest numbers on what others actually earn or make.
Employees who report a coworker's misconduct get outed or fear retaliation for having spoken up.
A toxic workplace culture, and the struggle to remove the toxic person poisoning it.
Coworkers cross personal boundaries by pulling pranks or messing with my workspace.
Developers are frustrated at being forced onto Windows laptops that aren't suited to development work.
The easy-apply pipeline is flooded with low-quality and AI-generated applications, so submissions become meaningless noise that vanish without response.
Employers can't find enough qualified candidates and the applications that do come in are weak.
Users who get the product for free feel entitled and give the worst feedback.
The company's public reputation and image are damaged in the eyes of outsiders.
A candidate's failure in a test gets misread as lack of ability when it's really nerves or the test environment, not the person.
People won't follow or read the instructions they're given.
Workers get fired for doing something completely reasonable — leaving at the end of their shift or interviewing for another job.
An interview ends abruptly and badly, with one side cutting it short or walking out.
Employees can't collect — or even clearly account for — the paid time off they already earned.
Workers leave jobs abruptly without giving proper notice.
AI-driven hiring tools like AI interviewers and recruiting software don't actually work, and people want companies to stop using them.
Honest creators are frustrated that their genuine work gets wrongly suspected or accused of being AI-generated.
People are unsure whether blocking ads on the client side is actually legally allowed.
People are stuck with bloated, heavy software when they just want a fast, lightweight native tool that does the job.
